source: Liu et al. (2026) Enforcing Code Reasoning in Agentic Scaffold for More Effective Issue Resolution (DeskCheck), study part
finding: Agents already reason about code in most trajectories. Trajectories with code reasoning resolve more issues, but this is a correlation. Agents do it unguided.
numbers: 7,955 trajectories, 6 scaffolds, 4 languages, SWE-bench Verified/Pro/Lite. Code reasoning seen in 66.95%. Resolution 69.84% with vs 50.81% without (14 trajectory sets pooled; chi-square significant per scaffold).
limits: Correlational. Harder tasks may both trigger reasoning and lower resolution, and detection of 'code reasoning' is by labelling.
agent_relevance: Supports an explicit 'trace the code' step in S1/S2, but the pooled gap is confounded by task difficulty.

source: Liu et al. (2026) DeskCheck: end-to-end results on SWE-bench Pro
finding: A scaffold that forces code reasoning at four stages (localise, repair-refine, audit vs issue text, validate by simulated input/expected output) beats two plain baselines on all three backbones.
numbers: 731 SWE-bench Pro instances. MiniMax-M3: 65.25% vs mini-SWE-Agent 54.72% (+10.53). GPT-5.6-Luna: 59.37% vs 53.08% (+6.29). Haiku-4.5: 51.16% vs Claude Code 42.82% (+8.34). Tokens +7.6% on average; cost $0.02-$0.28 more per instance. Significance tests p about 1e-11 to 1e-13. Rerunning baselines twice on DeskCheck-only wins recovered only 16/97, 7/49, 14/74, so 83.18% of gains not run noise.
limits: Different token budgets per arm (not strictly equal tokens, though close). It is a structured reasoning prompt plus audit stages, not a named comprehension strategy. Single paper, Oct 2026, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Closest thing to Gap 1: a stage-wise 'read and simulate' scaffold gives +6 to +10 points at small cost. Does not test bottom-up vs top-down.

source: Liu et al. (2026) DeskCheck ablation, stage by stage
finding: Turning code reasoning on one stage at a time raises resolution step by step. The validation stage adds the most.
numbers: 100-instance stratified subset, MiniMax-M3. Resolution 53% (all off), 56% (localise), 58% (+repair), 61% (+audit), 68% (full). Method-level recall 0.59, 0.65, 0.66, 0.67, 0.67; mini-SWE-Agent 53% and 0.57.
limits: Only 100 instances, so steps of 2-3 points are inside noise; only the total (53 to 68) is likely real. One model.
agent_relevance: Reasoning about inputs and expected outputs before writing a test is the biggest single piece. Fits an operator 'predict then check'.

source: Liu et al. (2026) DeskCheck vs execution-based reproduction (SWE-Doctor), localisation
finding: Simulating execution in the head localised faults better than actually running 28 reproduction tests. This is the head-to-head Gap 2 asked for, but only on localisation and with a different scaffold.
numbers: Average method-level recall with same LLMs: DeskCheck 0.66, mini-SWE-Agent 0.46, Claude Code 0.38, SWE-Doctor 0.23. SWE-Doctor ran 28.0 reproduction tests per instance. 107 Python instances: resolution 73.83 vs 57.94 (mini) vs 60.75 (SWE-Doctor) in one LLM block; 66.36 vs 57.01 vs 58.88 in another.
limits: Not a clean ablation: scaffolds differ in many ways, and SWE-Doctor environment set-up can fail. Does not show simulation beats execution in general; it shows structured simulation plus tests beats reproduction-test-only steering.
agent_relevance: Real execution is not automatically better; the quality of the reasoning around it matters. Keep both: simulate first, run when cheap.

source: Ugare and Chandra (2026) Agentic Code Reasoning (semi-formal reasoning)
finding: A fill-in certificate (premises, per-test execution trace, formal conclusion) beats free chain of thought on patch equivalence, code QA and fault localisation, without running code.
numbers: Patch equivalence curated pairs: 78.2% standard vs 88.8% semi-formal (steps 10.08 vs 28.17; equivalent-case accuracy 78.0 vs 93.0, non-equivalent 78.6 vs 82.9). Real agent patches 93%. RubberDuckBench code QA 87% vs 76% single-shot (+9 over agentic standard). Defects4J Top-5 +5 points.
limits: Semi-formal uses about 2.8x more steps, so it is not equal compute. Meta authors, single model family (Opus-4.5). No execution arm to compare with.
agent_relevance: A certificate template is a cheap structure that forces the agent to follow real call paths (it caught a shadowed function). Candidate for S1/S2 reading.

source: Lam et al. (2025) CodeCrash: exposing LLM fragility to misleading natural language in code reasoning (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Misleading comments, print statements and hints make LLM output prediction worse. Models treat comments as authoritative.
numbers: 1,279 questions from CRUXEval and LiveCodeBench, 17 LLMs. Average relative drop 23.2% (direct), 13.8% with chain of thought. Misleading comments and prints about 24% drop. GPT-4o-Mini misleading-comment drop -32.6% (CRUX) and -40.4% (LCB). Reasoning models use 2-3x tokens; 4 'reasoning collapse' events, all QwQ-32B on misleading hints.
quote: reducing relative performance degradation from 23.2% to 13.8% on average
limits: Output prediction on short functions, not review or repair. Comments here are obviously false in some variants.
agent_relevance: Direct answer to Gap 4 for LLMs: comments anchor models strongly. Mitigate with a rule: derive behaviour from code, treat comments as claims to check.

source: Lam et al. (2025) CodeCrash: identifier renaming alone
finding: Neutral renaming of identifiers (REN) costs little on CRUXEval but more on LiveCodeBench. Combined structural changes cost more than renaming alone.
numbers: REN relative drop on CRUX about -1% to -9% for most models (e.g. Haiku -3.8%); on LCB about -1% to -27% (e.g. Gemini-2.0-Flash -27.4%, Qwen2.5-7B -18.1%). Aggregated structural perturbation (PSC-ALL) larger: GPT-4o-Mini -27.9% / -31.9%.
limits: REN renames to neutral names but keeps the prompt unchanged. It does not test 'hide names on first read, then show names'.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly answered: the accuracy cost of hiding names is small on short code and larger on longer, harder code. No two-pass test exists yet.

source: Thornton (2026) LLM code reviewers are harder to fool than you think: adversarial comments
finding: For security review, adversarial comments (authority spoofing, dilution, technical deception) changed detection little. This contrasts with the strong anchoring seen in CodeCrash and in human data.
numbers: 100 samples x 8 comment variants x 8 models, 9,366 evaluations. Detection shifts -5% to +4%, McNemar p > 0.21, all CIs span zero. Baselines 89-96% commercial, 53-72% open source. Stating the finding as a verification hint: 96.9% detection, 47% of baseline misses recovered.
limits: Single run, security vulnerabilities only (pattern recognition against known classes), static comments, single-author preprint. Power about 80% for a 5-point effect.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for K14: comment anchoring depends on task. For known vulnerability patterns, strong models resist; for open-ended output prediction they do not.

source: Lin et al. (2026) How much static structure do code agents need? Deterministic anchoring
finding: Putting call and inheritance links into the code as plain comments helps a grep-style agent a little and makes it far more repeatable.
numbers: Codex baseline on SWE-bench Lite/Verified. Func@5 +2.2 points, 1.6 fewer interaction rounds, link-following rate 0.15-0.18 to 0.21-0.24, run-to-run variance roughly halved, Pass@1 +3.4 points on medium repos, about +10% input tokens. Denser tags show diminishing returns; large hub-heavy repos prefer inverse (who-calls-me) links only.
limits: Gains are small and scale dependent. Extra input tokens, so not equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: a call-graph hint is a cheap reading aid, useful mostly for stability. Prefer who-calls-me links.

source: Lin et al. (2026) preliminary head-to-head: graph agent vs grep agent
finding: A graph-tool agent (LocAgent) localised worse than a plain grep agent under matched settings.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, n=274. LocAgent File@1 0.726, File@5 0.861, Func@5 0.595. Codex grep-based File@1 0.912, File@5 0.967, Func@5 0.832.
limits: Different agent harnesses and model strength; not an isolated graph-vs-text test.
agent_relevance: Open-ended text search is hard to beat. Structure should be added as hints, not as a replacement tool.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) DualView: dual-modal structural reasoning for issue resolution
finding: Giving the agent graph views (module coupling, function call, class hierarchy, program dependence) as visual plus text helps across three agent systems.
numbers: SWE-bench Pro, 731 instances. Resolved 355 to 375 (+20), 316 to 351 (+35), 342 to 388 (+46). Full views 81 resolved vs 72-75 for single-view variants in an ablation.
limits: Needs a multimodal model for the visual side; base systems and cost differ. Contrasts with d10: graph as extra view works, graph as only tool does not.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: structure helps as an added view of the repo. Supports 'skeleton first, then dive'.

source: He and Roy (2026) SWE-Adept: depth-first agentic traversal and previews
finding: A two-agent system with agent-directed depth-first traversal over a code-structure tree, returning previews first, beats SWE-agent. Compact previews cut tokens and kept localisation about equal or slightly better.
numbers: Resolve rate SWE-agent 66.0% (Lite) and 39.5% (Pro) vs SWE-Adept 71.3% and 45.0%. Removing designed localisation: 69.0% / 43.3%; removing designed resolution: 68.7% / 41.5%. Preview+filter vs full code in search (table layout ambiguous): Func Acc@5 about 87.8% vs 87.2% with Claude-Sonnet-4.5 on Lite at 348k vs 393k tokens; about 63.3% vs 62.0% on Pro at 427k vs 502k.
limits: Table layout in the text extract is ambiguous; treat the token numbers as approximate. Depth-first is bundled with other changes, so it is not a Ko-and-Uttl style breadth vs depth test.
agent_relevance: Gap 5/6: preview-then-load-on-demand is the agent version of as-needed reading and saves 10-15% tokens.

source: Patel et al. (2026) PAUSE: one planning intervention at the first source-code edit
finding: Agents reach their first source edit at a median of 60% of the trajectory. One re-plan at that point, by a separate planner, beats rule-based stuck monitoring and matches periodic review at about 11-15% of the planner cost.
numbers: SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Qwen3-coder executor + GPT-5.6 Sol planner: +16.8% (OpenHands, Verified), +14.7% (SWE-agent, Multilingual). Versus LivePlan (rule-based repeat/stagnation monitor) +3.2% and +3.7%. Versus SICA (periodic) comparable at 11% and 15% planner cost. Offline: recovers 35.4% of eligible failed Verified tasks; resuming from prefix uses 33-41% fewer executor tokens.
limits: Gains are for a weak executor (Qwen3-coder) and a strong planner. Does not test step-count or repeat triggers on their own.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: the first-edit boundary is a cleaner trigger than repetition counts. It sits between the read states and the edit states.

source: von Mayrhauser and Vans (1995) Program comprehension during software maintenance and evolution, IEEE Computer 28(8)
finding: Primary text of the integrated metamodel. Hypotheses fail for three named reasons. Comprehension switches between top-down, situation and program models; no single prior model covers all behaviour. Experimental base is thin.
numbers: Hypothesis failure reasons: code to verify the hypothesis cannot be found; one piece of code satisfies different hypotheses (confusion); code cannot be explained. Beacons index into knowledge (swap in a loop signals sort; the name Sort). Keep the number of open hypotheses manageable. Review of experiments: only 1 used large-scale code, 2 medium-sized, 3 used C/Unix; most studied strategies, beacons, plans.
quote: No one model accounts for all behavior as programmers understand unfamiliar code.
limits: A review article; the numbers on the N=4 industrial subjects are in the companion SEJ paper, not here. Brooks's own paper still not opened.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 answered. Operators: (1) state a hypothesis, (2) search for beacon evidence, (3) on failure label which of the 3 reasons, (4) cap open hypotheses, (5) switch model when unrecognised code appears.

source: Tiemens (1989) Cognitive models of program comprehension (technical report summarising Brooks, Letovsky, Soloway)
finding: Secondary description of Letovsky: understanders ask why, how and data-description questions, form conjectures, and make inquiries; the steps are small and fragmented and need fast context switching.
numbers: Question types: why (trace up to the goal it serves), how (from goal down to code), data description. Letovsky events last seconds to minutes (meso scale).
limits: A 1989 student report. Not the Letovsky 1986 primary text, which stays unopened (paywalled).
agent_relevance: Why/how/what question types are easy operators for S1: ask 'why does this exist' and 'how is goal X done'.

source: Brooks (1983) Towards a theory of the comprehension of computer programs (via secondary summaries)
finding: Search results only: programmer forms a global hypothesis, refines it down, and checks it by looking for beacons. If none is found, revise or reject. Brooks ran no formal empirical test.
numbers: No numbers. Wiedenbeck (1985, 1986) later showed expertise relates to beacon recognition.
limits: Primary paper not opened (Elsevier paywall); statements come from search snippets of secondary sources.
agent_relevance: Beacon-then-revise rule is already captured by d14.

source: Abdelsalam, Peitek, Maurer, Toneva, Apel (2025) How do humans and LLMs process confusing code?
finding: LLM perplexity spikes line up with human EEG confusion signals at the level of small code regions, not whole snippets.
numbers: EEG data from 24 participants x 72 trials (Bergum et al.). Snippet-level perplexity higher for confusing code (effect sizes 0.42 average, 0.45 maximum, p<0.001). Region-level max perplexity vs late frontal positivity: Spearman 0.47 (p<0.001) for confusing code, 0.05 (p=0.664) for clean code. Data-driven spike detection overlapped labelled confusion atoms with rho 0.33 [0.12, 0.52] and also flagged other regions.
limits: One EEG dataset on small atom-of-confusion snippets. Correlation moderate; false positives on clean code.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: a perplexity spike on a small region is a usable 'look again here' flag; snippet-level perplexity is not.

source: Casalnuovo, Devanbu, Morgan (2020) Does language model surprisal measure code comprehension? (CogSci 2020, search snippet)
finding: Search snippet only: more surprising but meaning-equivalent code took participants longer to answer correctly.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; only the listing was seen.
agent_relevance: Supports surprisal as a difficulty signal for humans; see d17 for model-side use.

source: Uncertainty-aware self-correction for coding agents (ICLR 2026) and Ask or Assume (arXiv 2603.26233), search snippets
finding: Search snippets only: step-level uncertainty carried across a trajectory can trigger self-correction; a separate intent agent that detects under-specification raised SWE-bench Verified resolve rate.
numbers: Snippet claims: pass@1 up to +15.6 points (SWE-Rebench); 69.40% multi-agent vs 61.20% single agent (SWE-bench Verified, Sonnet 4.5).
limits: Not opened, numbers unverified. Triggers are uncertainty estimates, not step count or token surprisal.
agent_relevance: Gap 8/10: model-confidence triggers exist and may work better than step counts; verify before use.

source: Gap search negative result: explicit comprehension-strategy prompt vs plain prompt at equal tokens
finding: Several web and arXiv queries (the arXiv API was rate limited for part of the session) found no study that prompts agents with named bottom-up, top-down or as-needed strategies and compares them to plain reading at equal tokens. The nearest are DeskCheck (d02), SWE-Adept (d12) and semi-formal reasoning (d05).
numbers: None.
limits: Absence from limited search, not proof. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were at their free limits.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open; run the test ourselves (K01 agent_test).
